# AGENTS.md — AI for Health Equity Design Sprint (AWS)

Instructions for AI coding agents (OpenAI Codex and other AGENTS.md-compatible tools). These apply to every task in this repository. Follow them even when the user's request does not mention security.

---

# Event Context

You are assisting a participant in the **AI for Health Equity Design Sprint**, hosted by the Columbia University Data Science Institute (Frontiers in Data Science and AI initiative) with CUIMC, and supported by **Amazon Web Services (AWS)**.

- **The question:** can AI tools increase health access and equity? Teams design human-centered solutions for patients, clinicians, and advocates.
- **Community partners:** Community Service Society of New York (CSSNY) and Housing Works bring real-world access and equity challenges, advise teams, and judge the final projects.
- **Data:** teams work with **synthetic datasets** modeled on the partners' challenges.
- **Timeline:** kickoff and team formation on **Fri Nov 6, 2026**. Teams then build on their own for a week. Final **showcase on Fri Nov 13, 2026 (2:00–5:30 PM)**. Awards cover technical innovation, ethical rigor, and community engagement.
- **Teams are interdisciplinary.** The user may be a clinician, ethicist, policy student, or designer rather than a software engineer. Explain what you're doing in plain language, prefer simple readable code, and suggest small, testable steps.

## The AWS environment

- AWS access is a **temporary Innovation Sandbox account** with a spending limit. Participants sign in through an organizer-provided URL to **IAM Identity Center**, open the Innovation Sandbox app to see their lease, and get credentials in one of two ways: `aws sso login --profile hackathon` (preferred), or temporary keys copied from the access portal's **Access keys** window into their terminal as environment variables.
- **The account will be wiped** when the lease ends. Anything that exists only in the AWS account will be lost. Code, prompts, synthetic data, and notes belong in **git**, pushed to GitHub.
- The account is set up for **AI APIs**: Amazon Bedrock (Converse / ConverseStream / InvokeModel, Guardrails), Amazon Textract (synchronous), Amazon Polly, and Amazon Transcribe (streaming). Organizers may enable more. If a call returns `AccessDenied`, that service isn't enabled. Say so plainly and suggest a local alternative rather than trying workarounds.
- Region: `us-east-1`. Bedrock models are invoked with **US cross-Region inference profile IDs** (prefix `us.`).

## Run locally, spend on AI

- **Run and test the app on the participant's laptop** (Node.js / React / Python, or a local container). Local runs are free, fast to iterate on, and survive the account wipe.
- **Treat the budget as fuel for AI calls.** It goes furthest on model invocations, document extraction, and speech — the things that make the project work. Hosting, servers, databases, and storage cost money every hour and disappear at the wipe.
- When a cloud service seems useful, first offer the **local equivalent** (SQLite or a JSON file instead of a database, a local folder instead of S3, `npm run dev` or a container instead of hosting, Streamlit/Gradio on localhost for quick UIs). Mention roughly what the cloud option would cost and that it will be deleted.
- For the showcase, the demo runs from a laptop. If the user wants their project to live on after the event, show how the code maps to AWS Lambda + API Gateway (see the architecture guidance) and suggest they deploy it later in their own account.

## Choose the lower-cost option first

| Need | Lower-cost choice | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Text generation while building | Amazon Nova Micro or Nova Lite, Claude Haiku tier | Move to Claude Sonnet tier or Nova Pro only when quality needs it, such as for the final demo. |
| Search or RAG over documents | Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, with vectors stored locally (in memory, SQLite, FAISS, or Chroma) | You don't need a vector database service. |
| Reading documents | Textract `DetectDocumentText` | `AnalyzeDocument` costs more per page. Request only the feature types you use (FORMS, TABLES, QUERIES). |
| Speech output | Polly standard voices while building | Neural voices cost more. Switch for the demo. |
| Storing data | Local files, JSON, or SQLite | Survives the account wipe. |
| Hosting | `npm run dev` or a local container | Free, and the showcase demo runs from a laptop. |
| Repeated identical calls | Cache responses in a local file during development | Cuts both cost and waiting. |

## Warn before using expensive services

These bill by the hour or carry a high minimum charge whether or not anyone is using them. They are also deleted at the wipe.

- Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, and model customization (fine-tuning, continued pre-training)
- The largest models (for example the Claude Opus tier) or extended thinking, especially inside a loop over many records
- Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, which is also the default vector store when you create a Bedrock Knowledge Base
- Amazon Kendra
- Amazon SageMaker endpoints, notebooks, and Studio apps left running
- Amazon EC2 instances, especially GPU families (`g*`, `p*`, `inf*`, `trn*`)
- Amazon RDS / Aurora provisioned clusters, Amazon Redshift, Amazon EKS clusters, Amazon MSK
- NAT gateways, load balancers, and public IPv4 addresses
- AWS Marketplace subscriptions, Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances (never buy commitments in a sandbox)

If the user's plan needs one of these: stop, explain how it's billed, point them to the current price on the AWS pricing page (don't quote prices from memory), offer the lower-cost choice above, and continue only if they confirm.

# How You (the Coding Assistant) Should Behave

- **Git early, git often.** Suggest `git init` and a first commit at the start. After each working feature, and before the user stops for the day, remind them to commit and push to GitHub. Before any `git add`, have them check `git status` so secrets and data files stay out.
- **Ask before** running destructive or account-changing commands (deleting files, `git push --force`, any `aws` command that creates, changes, or deletes resources). Read-only calls and the AI APIs are fine.
- Before creating any AWS resource, explain what it costs, that it will be deleted at the wipe, and what the local alternative is. Then let the user decide.
- Never weaken security to "make it work" (disabling TLS verification, opening ports to `0.0.0.0`, committing secrets, adding `*` CORS with credentials). Explain the secure alternative instead.
- Keep cost visible: default to smaller models while iterating, and point out code that would call a model in a loop over many records.

# Data Handling — Synthetic Data Only

This environment is **not** approved for real health data. Treat these as hard rules:

1. **Only synthetic, fabricated, or public non-sensitive data.** The synthetic datasets provided by the organizers and community partners (CSSNY, Housing Works) are fine to use. Never request, accept, generate code to ingest, or store real PHI/PII (names, MRNs, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, SSNs, insurance IDs, images of real documents or people).
2. If data provided by the user **looks real** (realistic MRNs, real-looking names with DOBs, scanned documents with signatures), **stop and ask** the user to confirm it is synthetic before continuing.
3. When generating test data, make it **obviously synthetic**: use tools like Synthea or Faker, prefix IDs with `SYN-`, use fictional names, and add a `"synthetic": true` field or a header comment.
4. **Never log prompts, model responses, or document contents in full.** Log metadata (request ID, token counts, latency, error codes) instead. This mirrors HIPAA "minimum necessary" practice.
5. Don't place data files in public locations, gists, pastebins, or third-party services not listed above.
6. Note in the README that the project uses synthetic data and that production use with PHI would require a Business Associate Addendum (BAA), HIPAA-eligible services, and institutional (IRB/privacy/security) review.

> These practices are **HIPAA-aligned habits**, not HIPAA compliance. The hackathon environment is not a HIPAA-compliant environment.

# Security Baseline (AWS Well-Architected — Security Pillar)

## Identity & credentials
- **Never hard-code, print, commit, or ask the user to paste AWS credentials into code, files, or this chat.** Use the AWS SDK default credential chain. Two sources are fine:
  - `AWS_PROFILE=hackathon` from `aws sso login` (preferred; refreshes itself).
  - Temporary keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`) copied from the access portal's **Access keys** window and pasted into the user's terminal as environment variables. They expire, so tell the user to copy fresh ones and restart the app. When using them, `AWS_PROFILE` must be unset and removed from `.env`, because the JavaScript SDK prefers a profile over environment keys.
- Never write portal keys into `.env`, source files, notebooks, Dockerfiles, or `~/.aws/credentials`. If the user pastes keys into the chat, don't repeat or use them; tell them to keep keys in the terminal and to get fresh ones from the portal.
- Do not create IAM users, access keys, or Bedrock API keys. Do not suggest `aws configure` with static keys.
- Keep `.env`, `.aws/`, `*.pem`, and other secret files in `.gitignore`. Before suggesting `git add -A`, remind the user to check `git status`.
- **AWS SDK calls happen only in backend/server code.** Never put the AWS SDK or credentials in browser/React code.

## Encryption
- **In transit (preferred everywhere):** use HTTPS/TLS for every network call that leaves the laptop. AWS SDKs use TLS by default — never override endpoints to `http://` or disable certificate validation. Plain `http://127.0.0.1` is acceptable for local development only.
- **At rest (preferred):** keep local data on an encrypted disk (FileVault/BitLocker). If AWS storage is later enabled, keep **default encryption on**. **AWS-managed/default keys (e.g. SSE-S3, `aws/…` KMS keys) are acceptable** — customer-managed KMS keys are not required for this event.

## Least privilege & attack surface
- Bind local servers to `127.0.0.1`. Publish container ports as `-p 127.0.0.1:PORT:PORT`.
- Validate all inputs (type, length, file size, MIME type) before sending to an AWS API. Set request body limits.
- Set `maxTokens` on every model call; cap retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
- Return generic error messages to clients; log details server-side (without sensitive content).
- Add basic security headers (`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`).
- Prefer well-maintained dependencies; pin versions; run `npm audit` / `pip-audit` before demos. Ask before adding a new dependency.

## Generative AI specific
- Treat **model output as untrusted input**: render it as text (never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `eval`, or shell execution of model output) and validate any JSON against a schema.
- Treat **document/user content as untrusted** (prompt injection): keep system instructions in the `system` field, delimit user content clearly, and never let model output choose which tools, files or commands to run without validation.
- Use **Amazon Bedrock Guardrails** (`ApplyGuardrail` or `guardrailConfig`) where useful for PII filtering, denied topics, and content filters.
- Health apps must show a disclaimer: *"For demonstration only. Not medical advice. Synthetic data."* Keep a human in the loop for anything that resembles a clinical decision.

## Detection & traceability
- Log structured metadata (timestamp, route, model ID, token usage, latency, error name) to the console. Don't log full prompts or responses.

# App Architecture & Well-Architected Practices

## Preferred structure ("serverless-shaped, runs locally")
- `frontend/` — React (Vite). Calls only relative `/api/*` routes on its own backend.
- `backend/src/handler.js` — a **Lambda-style handler** `export const handler = async (event) => ({ statusCode, headers, body })` using API Gateway HTTP API (payload v2) event shape.
- `backend/src/local-server.js` — a thin Express adapter that converts HTTP requests to that event shape. Business logic stays in `handler.js`, not in Express.
- Create AWS SDK clients **once, outside the handler**. Read config (`MODEL_ID`, `AWS_REGION`) from environment variables.
- Optional container: multi-stage Dockerfile, non-root user, no secrets in the image, `.dockerignore` excluding `.env` and `node_modules`.

## Other Well-Architected pillars (lightweight for a hackathon)
- **Cost optimization:** spend the sandbox budget on AI API calls, not infrastructure. Run the app locally instead of hosting it. Default to smaller/cheaper models (Nova Micro/Lite, Claude Haiku tier) while iterating and switch up only when quality needs it; cache responses during development; avoid sending unnecessary context; process only the pages/records needed; test on a handful of records before running a batch.
- **Reliability:** handle `ThrottlingException` with backoff; set timeouts; fail gracefully with a user-visible message.
- **Performance:** stream responses (ConverseStream) for chat UIs; keep prompts concise.
- **Operational excellence:** a README with setup/run steps, `.env.example` with no secrets, and small commits pushed to GitHub frequently. The AWS account is wiped at the end, so the repo must be enough to rebuild and rerun everything (prompts, synthetic data generators, config).
- **Sustainability:** right-size models and avoid needless repeated calls.

## Equity & accessibility (what the judges look for)
- Design for the people the partner organizations serve: plain-language output (aim for about a 6th–8th grade reading level), and consider multiple languages and low-bandwidth or mobile use.
- Make the UI accessible: semantic HTML, labels on form fields, keyboard navigation, sufficient color contrast. Offer audio (Polly) or voice input (Transcribe) where it helps.
- Test prompts against varied synthetic personas (age, language, disability, housing status) and note where the model's output is weaker or biased for some groups.
- Keep a human in the loop and be clear about what the AI does and doesn't do. Document limitations in the README.

## AWS service usage hints
- Bedrock: prefer the **Converse API** (model-agnostic). Use `us.`-prefixed inference profile IDs.
- Textract: synchronous `DetectDocumentText` (lower cost) or `AnalyzeDocument` (forms/tables) with `Bytes` (images or single-page PDFs, max ~5 MB). This avoids needing S3.
- Polly: `SynthesizeSpeech` with `Engine: "standard"` while building; `"neural"` sounds better for the demo but costs more.
- Transcribe: streaming SDK only, proxied through the backend.

## Definition of done (check before the Nov 13 showcase)
- [ ] All work is committed and pushed to GitHub; a teammate can clone it and run it locally from the README
- [ ] The demo runs from a laptop (`npm run dev` or the local container) with nothing required in the AWS account except AI API access
- [ ] No credentials, `.env`, or real data in the repo (`git status`, `git log -p | grep -i key` spot check)
- [ ] All AWS calls server-side; browser calls only `/api/*`
- [ ] Inputs validated; `maxTokens` set; errors handled
- [ ] Model output rendered as text; disclaimer visible
- [ ] README states: synthetic data only; how to run; how it would deploy to AWS (Lambda + API Gateway + S3/CloudFront or Amplify)
- [ ] `npm audit` (or `pip-audit`) reviewed
